Recursion depth is indeed O(log n), but that only counts the *number* of calls — it does not multiply the work, because each level is half the size of the one above. worst_places.after: Put the two halves together. Each operation adds at most O(log n) to the potential, so over n operations the potential rises by at most O(n log n) in total. Every rotation costs O(1) and consumes some of that potential, so all rotations together also cost at most O(n log n). Divide by n operations: O(log n) rotation cost per operation on average. That is the same order as the height-update pass each operation already pays, so nothing gets worse — the per-operation amortized cost stays O(log n), not O(log² n. A single deletion can still fire O(log n) rotations; the average over the whole sequence is what is bounded.

worst_places.problem: algorithms-quiz-9. Options B ("BFS guarantees shortest path with O(V) space") and C ("BFS guarantees shortest path with O(V) queue space") are both true statements; the item asks for "most accurate" and then resolves the tie with a hand-wave the reader cannot verify. Compounding it: the explanation refers to "Option B" / "option C", but the four options are rendered as a plain list with no A/B/C/D labels, so the reader has to guess the mapping. This referencing habit appears in 12 of the 30 items, and the label style is not even consistent (algorithms-quiz-27 says "Option 1 ... Option 2 ... option 3", ru says «Вариант 1»; algorithms-quiz-10 says "Option A ... Option B", ru «Вариант A»).
worst_places.before: BFS explores level by level and guarantees the shortest path in unweighted graphs because it visits nodes in order of distance. The queue space is O(V) in worst case. DFS does not guarantee shortest path as it explores deeply first, potentially finding longer paths. Option B is imprecise about queue being the space requirement; option C correctly identifies BFS's guarantee.
worst_places.after: BFS guarantees the shortest path in an unweighted graph, and the memory it needs is the queue, which holds O(V) nodes in the worst case. BFS works because it visits nodes in order of distance from the source: everything one step away, then everything two steps away, and so on. So the first time it reaches the target, it cannot have taken a longer route. DFS goes as deep as it can before backing up, so the first route it finds to the target is often not the shortest. The other answers either name DFS as the one with the guarantee, or claim both traversals have it. (Options B and C should be rewritten so only one of them is true — as written both are correct statements.)

worst_places.quote:
2. Find odd-degree vertices in the MST (always an even count, by handshake lemma) and compute a minimum-weight perfect matching among them — cost ≤ half the optimal tour (proven via triangle inequality applied to the optimal tour split into two matchings).
3. Combine MST + matching into a multigraph — every vertex now has even degree, guaranteeing an Eulerian circuit exists.
worst_places.problem: algorithms-q-36 (en and ru). Two list items introduce six unexplained concepts in a row: odd-degree vertex, handshake lemma, minimum-weight perfect matching, multigraph, even degree, Eulerian circuit — plus a proof sketch compressed into a parenthesis. Nothing is grounded in an example and the final line then uses `OPT` as a symbol that is never introduced ("Total cost ≤ MST + matching ≤ OPT + OPT/2 = 1.5 * OPT"). MST is expanded on first use one line earlier, which makes the omission of OPT more jarring. With no theory article behind this bank, every one of those six terms is a stop-and-google.
worst_places.before:
2. Find odd-degree vertices in the MST (always an even count, by handshake lemma) and compute a minimum-weight perfect matching among them — cost ≤ half the optimal tour (proven via triangle inequality applied to the optimal tour split into two matchings).
3. Combine MST + matching into a multigraph — every vertex now has even degree, guaranteeing an Eulerian circuit exists.
worst_places.after:
2. Look at the vertices of the MST that have an odd number of edges. There is always an even number of them (every edge adds 1 to two vertices, so the degrees sum to an even number — the handshake lemma). Pair those odd vertices up so that every one of them gets exactly one partner and the total weight of the pairs is as small as possible; this is called a minimum-weight perfect matching. Its cost is at most half the optimal tour: the optimal tour visits these vertices in some cyclic order, and splitting that cycle into alternating edges gives two matchings, so the cheaper one costs at most half.
3. Add those matching edges on top of the MST. Because each odd vertex just gained one more edge, every vertex now has an even number of edges. A connected graph where every vertex has even degree has an Eulerian circuit — a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once. (Write `OPT` out on first use: "call the total weight of the optimal tour OPT".)

patterns: No answer in the question bank ever traces its own code. Across all 40 answers there are zero worked examples — no `console.log`, no "for input [3,1,4] the state after step 2 is …", no input → intermediate state → output walk-through; only one answer (algorithms-q-19) contains a concrete data literal in its prose at all. Every code block is a finished implementation dropped in whole, and 19 of the 40 have no inline comments either (algorithms-q-3, q-5, q-7, q-9 through q-20). The prose then asserts the invariant the code maintains ("the path from head to the meeting point is equal in length to the path from the meeting point back around to the cycle's start" — algorithms-q-12) and moves on. A reader who cannot already run the algorithm mentally has no way in. This is the highest-leverage fix in the zone: 3-5 lines of trace per answer, using the existing code unchanged.

Big-O is explained where it is easy and asserted where it is hard — the explanation quality falls off exactly as difficulty rises. The junior tier is genuinely good: algorithms-q-3 says "each step cuts the search space in half … for an array of a million elements, you need at most ~20 comparisons instead of up to a million", which is precisely what the rubric asks for. From the senior tier on, the plain-words reason disappears and the notation carries the argument alone: algorithms-q-38 restates its own bound three times without ever saying what the potential function buys, algorithms-q-36 hands over `OPT + OPT/2 = 1.5 * OPT` with `OPT` undefined, algorithms-q-37 gives `O(log_B n)` cache lines with no sense of scale. The honourable exception proves it can be done at any level — algorithms-q-24 explains α(n) as "under 5 for any n you could ever represent in memory". That register needs to be pushed up into the senior and advanced tiers.

The quiz bank was written to a different standard than the question bank and needs its own pass. Its explanations reference options by labels the reader never sees ("Option B", "option C" in 12 of 30 items, and inconsistently — "Option 1/2/3" in algorithms-quiz-27, «Вариант A/B» in quiz-10, «Вариант 1/2» in quiz-27). Its ru is a calque layer the question-bank ru does not have ("пространство" 23× for memory, «доминирующий термин», «коллидируют», «приоритизируется»). And it carries three correctness defects the reader cannot detect without theory: two wrong answer keys (quiz-14, quiz-16), a self-contradicting derivation (quiz-16), an unresolvable duplicate-option pair (quiz-9), and a pre-order traversal labelled in-order (quiz-8) contradicting quiz-23.
